item.title: 4 Best Ways to Check a Legal Contract Using Neural Networks
item.description:
You have a PDF in your inbox, need to sign it by six today, and your lawyer is on vacation. We tested one file using four different methods to see where neural networks can help check a legal contract right up to the signature. In November 2025, Avito and Pravo.ru, in a joint survey, collected responses from over 500 lawyers. 88% use AI in their work, 63% report increased productivity, and 39% trust neural networks for drafting and checking standard documents and contracts. However, 84% fear inaccurate responses, and 80% say every result still needs to be read by a human. Now, let's see how neural networks and services handle legal documents. Can AI detect tricky clauses in a document? Read more

item.title: RAG with Access Rights: How to Prevent an Employee from Seeing a Document They Shouldn't
item.description:
A practical breakdown of a solution using a real corporate FAQ bot. A shift supervisor at a warehouse opens the corporate AI assistant and types: "What should be done if a driver is late with a delivery?" A few seconds later, an answer appears – clear, correct, with a link to the source: the logistics operations regulations. It can be downloaded. Now, imagine the same employee asks another question: "How much do we pay carriers per kilometer?" There's nothing stopping them from asking this. What matters is what happens next. If the file with the rate schedule is in the same database as the regulations, the assistant will respond politely, accurately, and attach a download link. This is the problem. We've solved semantic search and achieved good answers. But the next complex task is to ensure the assistant only answers based on what a specific person is permitted to know. Read more

item.title: I wanted my own system that I could change at any time, so I made three desktop AI applications
item.description:
I've always wanted to have my own system: my own applications where I can change anything, not someone else's, which they might change tomorrow. This is how Zeqou came about – three desktop applications for working with language models: the ZeqouXChat chat on Tauri 2 and React 19, the Zeqou Harness workspace for agents with a task list and memory, and the ZeqouXTraining model fine-tuning studio with LoRA, QLoRA, and a Thinking mode. I'll explain how it all works, what problems I encountered (spoiler: installers), and why I chose a closed license. Read more

item.title: The Evolution of AI Harness
item.description:
Over the past few years, the wrapper around LLM models has evolved from a simple chat interface and a rules file in an editor to a self-sufficient technological layer – the harness – with its own protocols, standards, and foundation. Client lock-in has shifted from the specific LLM model level to this harness level. Definitions: 1. Model – an LLM, a neural network that generates text on demand. It is stateless (doesn't remember previous calls), has no access to the external world, and is incapable of action – only generating the next token or a probable set of phrases based on the input context. 2. Harness – the software and infrastructure wrapper around the model, transforming it from a text generator into a system capable of performing "meaningful" actions. The harness provides the model with functionality: tools (access to the external world), context management (memory, sessions, compaction), rules/instructions (behavior), permissions and rights (security), and optionally enhancements – hooks, skills, orchestration. The harness is the "body," the model is the "semantic brain." 3. AI Agent – a model placed within a harness, thus capable of acting, i.e., perceiving the environment's state through tools, maintaining context between steps, planning, and executing multi-step tasks. An agent is not a component but the result of combining a model and a harness. Below is an approximate account of the development of harness ideas and its current state. Read more

item.title: A Quarter Century Until Vibe Coding...
item.description:
In 2000, I was writing assembly code for satellite tracking device verification, convinced that serious systems were built solely by hand. Vibe coding was still 25 years away. Now I'm 50. Since then, I've spent most of my time writing software for hardware: ship control systems, avionics test complexes, heat meters, intercoms, and most recently, equipment for self-service car washes. I always designed my systems' architecture myself and wrote the low-level firmware too. But beyond that, I became dependent on others. Servers, web interfaces, documentation: each required a separate person, whom I'd have to find and pay, and then wait. Until everything was assembled, my architecture existed only on paper, and no matter how much I called myself an architect, I had nothing to show. I viewed AI the same way most engineers I knew did: a toy. Good for whipping up a landing page, writing a poem, or at best, a script. The term 'vibe coding' meant to me: someone doesn't understand what they're doing and hopes the model will somehow do it for them. People I respected didn't involve AI in serious projects, and neither did I. I started experimenting out of desperation: the company had no developers left, but there were two hundred devices to support. I had to use AI for all development, including tasks that previously would have required a whole team. And then I discovered it's long past being a toy. You set a task, define the architecture, and it performs as a competent programmer would. Read on

item.title: Twelve Days of an AI Agent on a Live B2B Portal: What It Found and Where It Can't Be Trusted
item.description:
Twelve working days of an AI agent on a live b2b portal: exchange with 1C on schedule, real managers, active orders. Four quiet exchange failures it resolved (zero from 1C instead of price, trailing space in order number, double nightly export, unbuilt showcase), and four areas where the agent cannot be trusted. Regarding failures, the interesting part isn't the fix, but how they were noticed: half of the tasks were never assigned to it. Regarding errors, they are repetitive, and a specific safeguard had to be implemented for each. Read on.

item.description:

item.title: How to Quickly Convert an Image to Excel
item.description:
A 300 IQ supplier sends a price list not as a file, but as a photo of a sheet. The accounting department asks to enter data from a receipt or report that exists only as a scan into a table. Previously, the only option was to sit down and retype everything manually, line by line. Now, all you need is a chat with a neural network. Upload the photo, write one short request, and get a ready-made table that you can just paste into Excel. We show with three real examples how to do this and what to pay attention to, so that the numbers at the output don't diverge from what was in the photo. Read more

item.title: Triage of Vulnerabilities in AI Platforms: Why Calendar SLA Broke and What to Use Instead
item.description:
On June 10, 2026, CISA released directive BOD 26-04, replacing BOD 19-02 and BOD 22-01. The new directive shifts from fixed deadlines for vulnerabilities in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog to a risk-based approach for prioritizing security updates. CISA now considers asset public accessibility, KEV status, exploitability automation, and attack impact. The new model, based on SSVC, mandates a 3-day fix for the most urgent cases and allows for scheduled updates for the least urgent. However, AI platforms present a challenge due to the diverse nature of "fixing" vulnerabilities across different layers (web API, ML dependencies, GPU runtime, inference engine, model weights). A uniform CVSS score does not equate to uniform priority, timeline, or remediation strategy. This article analyzes eight public CVEs from a typical AI stack using a decision tree, examining asset accessibility, exploitation evidence, exploit automation, technical impact, and actual remediation paths. It also demonstrates how to derive decision thresholds from FIRST's published data. The content is intended for AppSec and DevSecOps engineers managing platform vulnerability backlogs, team leads whose releases depend on security tickets, and CISOs. A dedicated section addresses FSTEC requirements for Russian CISOs. The approach is also applicable to standard infrastructure without GPUs and models, with adjustments to the asset inventory but not the prioritization logic.

item.title: We Wrote an Autonomous Agent for VACUUM/ANALYZE and Launched it on 800+ Test Databases: What Came of It
item.description:
How to simplify the management of a fleet of 800+ PostgreSQL database instances? You can customize postgres_exporter to get the metrics you need. Or, for an even simpler approach, monitor using Grafana, Prometheus, and a customized postgres_exporter, and get data through an AI report that aggregates Prometheus data via direct PromQL queries. But if that's not enough, you can even entrust an AI agent with typical tickets like freeing up disk space and scheduling database shutdowns. My name is Stanislav Epishin, and I'm from the "R4C.Support.Apocalypse Riders" team at SberTech. I've previously written about how we customized postgres_exporter to pangolin_exporter, fixing a bug in transaction duration calculation, and how we implemented the Prometheus + Pipeliner + TaskTracker + GigaChat stack for automatic ticket creation. In this article, I'll discuss an R&D project for a small DBA team where we tested a hypothesis: can we build an autonomous agent that will independently handle tickets, such as clearing disk space, performing VACUUM/ANALYZE, and scheduling database shutdowns? Here, I've outlined instructions for creating the agent (with full code and explanations) and a detailed real-world example of autonomous VACUUM/ANALYZE with anomaly detection via LLM. I'll also show how to organize an event feed for monitoring the agent's operation and delve into where and how LLM is used in the project. Read on
